publication_scope.blurb: Louis Le Blanc de Beaulieu - Sedan Theological Theses, newly rendered from the 1675 London Latin. Covers De Theologia through Angelorum & Hominum Sanctorum Cultu Romana I-LXXVII and Pars Secunda (Reformata) I-CI, De Primi Hominis Immortalitate I-XXXV, De Justitia Primi Hominis I-LIX, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio in genere I-XLVIII, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio absolute & in se spectato (Scholae Romanae doctrina I-XLIX; Pars Tertia I-XLIII), the theses on reconciling divine concurrence with human freedom I-LIX, on human freedom and divine foreknowledge I-XLIV, and on human freedom and the divine decrees, Part One (middle knowledge) I-LXV, Part Two (the Roman doctors) I-XXXVI and Part Three (the Reformed) I-LI, and on how fallen man's free choice stands toward saving good (I-LX), and on the necessity of grace for moral good in fallen man (Pars Prior I-LIII; Pars Posterior, the Protestant doctrine, I-LIX), and on the various distinctions and senses of grace in the Roman School (I-LXX) and in the Reformed Schools (I-XLIX), and on the Roman School's division of grace into sufficient and efficacious (I-CXLV, complete), and on the Protestant doctrine of that distinction, the Lutherans of the Augsburg Confession, the Remonstrants, and the Reformed who subscribe to Dort, with the Reformed debate on how grace moves the will, Le Blanc's concluding comparisons and an appendix on the Socinians (I-LXXXVIII, complete), and on whether and how far man can fulfil the Law by Christ's grace (I-XXXIII). Not the collected folio.
publication_scope.era_note: Le Blanc wrote in the mid-seventeenth century as Reformed professor at the Academy of Sedan. This is not a patristic work. It is a public-domain Latin Reformed retrieval on the same Fathers-site pipeline. The 1675 Pitt folio is Public Domain Mark 1.0. Do not treat the site as ante-Nicene only.

source_text: XIX. Quin illud ipsum obsequium quod fideles legi exhibent suis defectibus & naevis non caret, & in illis ipsis operibus quae conformiter legi edunt summam ἀκρίβειαν, legis non assequuntur; semperque illo respectu restat iis materia profectus, & aliquid ad quod contendere debeant. Quod evidens est Pauli Apost. exemplo. Neque enim facile reperietur aliquis cui tantam gratiae mensuram indulserit Christus. Et tamen ipse fatetur se nondum esse perfectum, & se ad ulteriora perpetuo contendere. Phil. 3. Non inquit, quod jam apprehenderim, aut jam perfectus sim: sequor autem, si quo modo comprehendam, in quo & comprehensus sum a Christo Jesu. Fratres, ego me non arbitror comprehendisse. Unum autem ago, quae quidem retro sunt obliviscens, ad ea vero quae sunt priora me extendens, ad destinatum persequor, ad bravium supernae vocationis Dei in Christo Jesu.
english: Thesis XIX. Even the obedience believers give the law has its own defects and flaws. In the very works they do in conformity with the law they fall short of the law's full exactness (ἀκρίβεια), so that in this respect there is always room left for progress, always something still to strive toward.

Paul's example makes this plain. It would be hard to find anyone to whom Christ gave so large a measure of grace, yet Paul admits he is not yet perfect and keeps reaching for what lies further on. In Philippians 3 he writes: 'Not that I have already grasped it, or am already perfect; but I press on, if somehow I may take hold of that for which Christ Jesus took hold of me. Brothers, I do not consider that I have taken hold of it. One thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and stretching out toward what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal, for the prize of God's upward call in Christ Jesus.'

source_text: XX. At, inquies, Apostolus ipse eo in loco supponit quosdam esse perfectos, & se in eorum numero collocat. Verbis enim citatis subjungit, quicunque ergo perfecti sumus hoc sentiamus. Et 1 Cor. 2. Sapientiam, inquit, loquimur inter perfectos. Multisque viris sanctis in scriptura testimonium perhibetur quod perfecti fuerint. Ita de Noe dicitur Gen. 6. Noe vir justus fuit atque perfectus in generationibus suis, & ambulavit cum Deo. Et de Job Deus ipse Satanam alloquens dicit, Nunquid considerasti servum meum Job, quod non sit ei similis in terra, Isch Tham, i. Vir integer, sive, perfectus, & rectus, ac timens Deum, & recedens a malo? cap. 1. & 2. Imo David, Psal. 18. non veretur sibi talem perfectionem tribuere. Fui, inquit, immaculatus, sive perfectus, cum eo, & custodivi me ab iniquitate mea. Et retribuit mihi Dominus secundum justitiam meam, & secundum puritatem manuum mearum in conspectu oculorum ejus.
english: Thesis XX. Someone will object that in that very passage the apostle assumes some people are perfect and counts himself among them. Right after the words just quoted he adds, 'Let as many of us as are perfect think this way.' In 1 Corinthians 2 he says, 'We speak wisdom among the perfect.'

Scripture also testifies of many holy men that they were perfect. Of Noah, Genesis 6 says: 'Noah was a righteous man and perfect in his generations, and he walked with God.' Of Job, God himself says to Satan in chapters 1 and 2: 'Have you considered my servant Job, that there is no one like him on earth, Isch Tham, that is, a man of integrity, or perfect, and upright, who fears God and turns away from evil?'

David in Psalm 18 does not even shrink from claiming such perfection: 'I was blameless, or perfect, with him, and kept myself from my iniquity. And the Lord repaid me according to my righteousness, according to the cleanness of my hands in his sight.'

source_text: XXI. Quae difficultas ut solvatur observanda est duplex perfectionis distinctio. Est enim perfectio quaedam absolute sic dicta, alia vero secundum quid & comparate tantum. Absolute perfectum est illud cui in suo genere nihil deest. Comparate vero perfecta dicuntur ea quae licet a summa perfectione absint, multa tamen superant alia ejusdem generis, cum quibus instituitur eorum comparatio. Quum dicimus in hac vita nullos esse perfectos, sive qui perfectum divinae voluntati obsequium praebeant, istud intelligimus de perfectione absoluta, quae pervenit ad summum, & ad quam nihil addi potest, quo sensu Paulus agnoscit se nondum esse perfectum, quia nondum pervenerat ad illum gradum amoris & obsequii erga Deum, ad quem evecti sunt beati spiritus cum Christo regnantes; quorum non tantum cognitio, sed obsequium etiam & amor, nullum amplius potest sumere incrementum, cum totis omnino viribus, totoque voluntatis affectu ferantur in Deum. Verum hoc non obstat quo minus fideles qui virtute caeteris praecellunt, & qui in veritatis divinae notitia, & pietatis ac justitiae studio majores progressus fecerunt, perfecti nominentur, non quidem simpliciter, sed respectu eorum qui multum illis hac in parte cedunt, quique sunt adhuc, ut Paulus loquitur, infantes in Christo, & quodammodo carnales, prae illis qui singulari ratione spirituales appellantur, ut videre est 1 Cor. 3. Et hi sunt inter Christianos, ut sic dicam, adultiores, & aetatis ac staturae, si ita loqui licet, magis provectae, quos Paulus locis ante citatis perfectos vocat, dum ait, Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos, &, Quicunque perfecti sumus hoc sentiamus.
english: Thesis XXI. To resolve this difficulty we need a twofold distinction of perfection. One kind is called perfection absolutely; the other is perfection only in a certain respect, by comparison. What is absolutely perfect lacks nothing in its kind. Things are called perfect by comparison when, though far short of the highest perfection, they still surpass many other things of the same kind with which they are compared.

When we say that no one in this life is perfect, that is, no one gives God's will a perfect obedience, we mean absolute perfection: perfection that has reached the top and can receive no addition. In this sense Paul admits he is not yet perfect, since he had not yet reached the degree of love and obedience toward God to which the blessed spirits reigning with Christ have been raised. Their knowledge, and their obedience and love as well, can grow no further, because they are carried toward God with all their powers and the whole affection of their will.

None of this stops believers who outstrip others in virtue, and who have advanced further in knowing divine truth and in striving after piety and righteousness, from being called perfect. They are perfect not simply, but relative to those who fall well behind them here: those who are still, in Paul's words, infants in Christ and in some way carnal, compared with others who are called spiritual in a special sense (see 1 Corinthians 3). These are, so to speak, the grown-ups among Christians, of a riper age and stature, if one may put it so. They are the ones Paul calls perfect in the passages cited, when he says, 'We speak wisdom among the perfect,' and, 'Let as many of us as are perfect think this way.'

source_text: XXII. Huic distinctioni affinis est altera, juxta quam distingui solet perfectio in perfectionem partium & perfectionem graduum. Perfecta secundum gradus obedientia illa est quae attingit summum perfectionis gradum, & per quam aliquis legi ita perfecte se conformat & subjicit, ut in eo nihil prorsus desiderari queat, neque hoc respectu possit in melius proficere. Hac ratione contendimus, & per se manifestum est legem a nullo perfecte in hac vita impleri. Verum obedientia quae multum a summo gradu perfectionis abest, nihilominus esse & dici potest perfecta secundum partes; quoniam respectu partium, sive essentialium, sive integrantium, nihil illi deest eorum quae necessaria sunt ut sit obedientia vera & Deo accepta. Hoc sensu perfecta est obedientia piorum in hac vita, & hoc respectu fideles qui sunt per Christi gratiam renovati, & spiritu illius ducuntur, perfecte Dei legem implere possunt, id est, verum & sincerum, Deoque gratum obsequium mandatis illius praebere. Nec enim essentialis ejusmodi perfectio aliud est quam ipsius rei veritas atque sinceritas.
english: Thesis XXII. Close to this distinction is another, which commonly divides perfection into perfection of parts and perfection of degrees. Obedience perfect in degree reaches the highest degree of perfection: through it a person conforms and submits himself to the law so perfectly that nothing at all can be found lacking in him and he can make no further improvement in that respect. In this sense, as we maintain and as is self-evident, no one fulfils the law perfectly in this life.

Obedience that falls well short of the highest degree can still be, and be called, perfect in its parts. As to its parts, essential or integral, it lacks none of what is needed for true obedience acceptable to God. In this sense the obedience of the godly in this life is perfect, and in this respect believers renewed by Christ's grace and led by his Spirit can fulfil God's law perfectly: that is, they can give his commandments a true, sincere obedience that pleases God. The essential perfection of such a thing is simply its being true and sincere.

source_text: XXIII. Ut autem istud clarius innotescat, observandum est ad hoc, ut obedientia nostra vera & sincera sit, tria praecipue requiri. Primum est ut praestetur non tantum corpore & opere externo, sed interno quoque animi affectu. Neque enim quicquam prodest ea facere quae lex jubet, nisi id fiat ex Dei amore, & voluntatis illius implendae ac gloriae ejus promovendae studio. Ut nec satis est quendam affectum Deo obsequendi habere, nisi mandata ejus, quum res id postulat, ipso opere compleantur. Praeterea non sufficit ad veram obedientiam ut quaedam Dei mandata, reliquis neglectis, servemus: sed necesse est ut omnibus legis Divinae praeceptis nos serio subjiciamus, illaque, cum sese offert occasio, implere studeamus. Denique debet esse obedientia nostra constans & perseverans: Nec satis est Deo ad tempus obsequi, sed in ejus obsequio, tam per res adversas quam per res secundas, ad finem usque perseverandum est.
english: Thesis XXIII. To make this clearer, note that three things above all are needed for our obedience to be true and sincere. First, it must be given not only with the body and outward action but with the inner affection of the mind as well. Doing what the law commands profits nothing unless it springs from love of God and from zeal to carry out his will and advance his glory. Equally, a certain wish to obey God is not enough unless his commandments are actually carried out in deed when the situation calls for it.

Second, true obedience is not satisfied by keeping some of God's commandments while neglecting the rest. We must earnestly submit to every precept of the divine law and try to fulfil each one as occasions arise. Third, our obedience must be steady and lasting. Obeying God for a while is not enough; we have to persevere in obeying him to the end, in hard times as in good ones.

source_text: XXIV. Horum omnium respectu nihil deest obedientiae eorum qui vere pii & per spiritum Dei regeniti sunt. Nec enim corpore tantum Deo serviunt, sed mentem & affectus voluntati ejus subjiciunt. Nec solum opere praestant quae lege praecipiuntur; sed etiam in eo gloriam Dei spectant, & amore illius moventur. Non his, aut illis mandatis duntaxat obedire satagunt; sed universae legi Dei & singulis ejus mandatis sese conformare nituntur. Nec solum ad aliquod tempus, & quandiu res prospere fluunt, sed etiam quum ingruunt tentationes & persecutiones, & ad ultimum usque vitae spiritum mandata Dei ob oculos habent, & actiones suas ad eorum normam exigunt.
english: Thesis XXIV. On all these counts, the obedience of the truly godly, those reborn by God's Spirit, lacks nothing. They serve God not with the body alone but bring mind and affections under his will. They not only do in deed what the law commands; in doing it they aim at God's glory and are moved by love for him.

Their concern is not to obey merely this or that commandment; they try to conform themselves to God's whole law and to every one of its commandments. And they do so not merely for a while, as long as things go well, but also when temptations and persecutions break upon them: to their last breath they keep God's commandments before their eyes and measure their actions by that rule.

source_text: XXV. Itaque jure merito potest eorum obedientiae tribui perfectio illa, quae perfectio Partium in Scholis appellari solet. Siquidem integrae legi, & universis illius praeceptis, tum corporis actus, tum animi affectus, idque constanter & perseveranter exigere conantur. Et certe, nisi hoc esset, scriptura fidelibus non tribueret justitiam & sanctitatem veram, dum ait, illos indui novo homine, qui creatur secundum Deum, in justitia & sanctitate veritatis, Ephes. 4. Nam vera justitia non est, quae respectu partium, ad essentiam justitiae omnino pertinentium, manca & mutila est. Et haec est illa perfectio cujus nomine laudantur Job & Noe, & quam David sibi ipsi tribuere non formidat. Etenim per perfectionem solum ibi designatur integritas atque sinceritas sanctorum istorum virorum. Siquidem vox Hebraea Tham sive thamim, quam ibi Interpretes per perfectum exponunt, integrum & sincerum proprie significat.
english: Thesis XXV. So the perfection the Schools usually call perfection of parts can rightly be ascribed to their obedience. They try to bring both the acts of the body and the affections of the mind into line with the whole law and every one of its precepts, and to do so steadily and with perseverance.

If this were not so, Scripture would certainly not credit believers with true righteousness and holiness, as it does in Ephesians 4 when it says they put on the new man, created after God in the righteousness and holiness of truth. A righteousness maimed and mutilated in the parts that belong to its very essence is no true righteousness.

This is the perfection for which Job and Noah are praised and which David has no qualms about claiming for himself. In those places 'perfection' means only the integrity and sincerity of these holy men; the Hebrew word Tham or thamim, which translators there render 'perfect', properly means whole and sincere.

source_text: XXVI. Negamus igitur fideles perfecte Dei legem implere posse, si sermo sit, de perfectione quae absoluta dicitur & graduum: tum quia omnes illi, non minus quam caeteri homines, per naturam sunt peccatores; tum quia post acceptam gratiam non desinunt in multis offendere, & gravibus etiam lapsibus obnoxii manent: neque in bonis ipsis operibus quae faciunt summam illam ἀκρίβειαν, quam lex in rigore suo exigit, assequuntur. Et tamen cum scriptura dicimus & docemus, fideles Dei mandata per Christi gratiam servare, & aliquo etiam modo legem implere, quoniam veram Deoque probatam obedientiam legi divinae, secundum omnia illius praecepta, exhibent: quae obedientia licet multum infra summam perfectionem subsidat, nihilominus, juxta scripturae stylum, perfecta dici potest; quoniam vera atque sincera est, nec quicquam ei deest eorum quae ad obedientiae verae & Deo acceptae, naturam & integritatem necessario requiruntur.
english: Thesis XXVI. So we deny that believers can fulfil God's law perfectly, if the perfection meant is the one called absolute, the perfection of degrees. All of them, no less than other people, are sinners by nature; even after receiving grace they keep stumbling in many things and stay exposed to serious falls; and in their good works themselves they fall short of the full exactness (ἀκρίβεια) the law demands in its strictness.

Yet with Scripture we say and teach that believers keep God's commandments by Christ's grace, and in a certain way fulfil the law as well, since they give the divine law a true obedience, approved by God, that covers all its precepts. That obedience sits far below the highest perfection, but in Scripture's usage it can still be called perfect, because it is true and sincere and lacks nothing that the nature and integrity of true obedience, acceptable to God, necessarily requires.

source_text: XXVII. Atque haec Sententiae Orthodoxae explicatio diligenter observanda est propter doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, qui in hac quaestione, ut in multis aliis, Scholae Reformatae doctrinam, aut non intelligunt, aut studio pervertunt. Siquidem Theologis Protestantibus tribuunt quod simpliciter negent Christi fideles Dei mandata servare posse, & legem ita implere, ut quaedam eorum opera justa appellari possint. Imo quod doceant legem plane impossibilem esse homini etiam per Christi gratiam justificato: adeo ut non possit ulla bona opera facere, nec in eo sit ulla vera actualis justitia. Sicut videre est apud Bell. de Justif. lib. 4. cap. 10. & apud Becanum in summa Theologiae Scolasticae, tom. 2. tract. 4. cap. 4. cujus titulus est, De merito bonorum operum ex sententia Calvinistarum.
english: Thesis XXVII. This account of the orthodox view needs careful attention because of the doctors of the Roman Church, who on this question, as on many others, either fail to understand the teaching of the Reformed school or twist it deliberately. They ascribe to Protestant theologians a flat denial that Christ's faithful can keep God's commandments and fulfil the law in such a way that any of their works can be called righteous.

They even claim that Protestants teach that the law is simply impossible for someone justified by Christ's grace, so that he can do no good works at all and has no true actual righteousness. This can be seen in Bellarmine, De justificatione, book 4, chapter 10, and in Becanus's Summa of scholastic theology, volume 2, tractate 4, chapter 4, which is titled 'On the merit of good works according to the opinion of the Calvinists'.

source_text: XXVIII. Unde est quod, hac falsa nitentes hypothesi, cum inter nos & ipsos controversiae statum ponunt qui plane nullus est, hunc scilicet, Utrum homines justificati, & gratia Domini adjuvante, possint ita legem divinam implere, ut opera ipsorum, non modo non sint appellanda peccata, sed etiam vere ac proprie justa dici mereantur. Quae sunt verba Bellarmini capite illo 10. jam citato. Quibus conformia sunt quae leguntur apud Gabrielem Vasquez tom. 2. in 1. 2. disp. 212. cujus titulus est, An justi homines possint ita adimplere legem, ut ipsorum opera, non modo non sint peccata, sed etiam justa dicenda sint.
english: Thesis XXVIII. Hence, resting on this false assumption, they frame between us and them a state of the controversy that does not exist at all, namely 'whether justified people, helped by the Lord's grace, can fulfil the divine law in such a way that their works not only should not be called sins but truly and properly deserve to be called righteous.' These are Bellarmine's words in the chapter 10 already cited.

In line with them is what we read in Gabriel Vasquez, volume 2 on the Prima Secundae, disputation 212, whose title asks 'whether righteous people can fulfil the law in such a way that their works are not only not sins but are to be called righteous.'

source_text: XXIX. Verum nunquam fuit animus Protestantium quicquam horum negare. Non docent justificatis legem Dei esse plane impossibilem. Non inficiantur fideles veram Dei mandatis praestare obedientiam, & legem Dei per Christi gratiam sic a piis impleri, ut opera bona faciant. Nec dicunt opera, quibus divino spiritu movente legi se conformare student, appellanda esse peccata, & revera talia natura sua esse: sed fatentur illa posse & debere sancta & justa dici. Id solum ab ipsis est perpetuo negatum, a fidelibus legem impleri posse perfecte, quia illorum obedientia, quamvis vera & sincera sit, longe tamen a summa perfectione semper abest.
english: Thesis XXIX. Protestants never meant to deny any of this. They do not teach that God's law is simply impossible for the justified. They do not deny that believers give God's commandments true obedience, or that by Christ's grace the godly fulfil God's law to the extent of doing good works.

Nor do they say that the works by which believers, moved by the divine Spirit, try to conform themselves to the law must be called sins and are really sins by nature; they grant that such works can and should be called holy and righteous. The one thing they have always denied is that believers can fulfil the law perfectly, since their obedience, however true and sincere, always falls far short of the highest perfection.

source_text: XXX. Ac nequis calumnietur Protestantes diversum sentire, & nos alienam ipsis affingere doctrinam, hac de re quaedam eorum testimonia velut in specimen proferemus. Nam singula persequi infinitae operae, & superfluum esset. Et res alioqui est attendenti per se satis manifesta. Igitur Paraeus scribens in Bellar. lib. 4. de Justif. cap. 10. In quaestione, inquit, est, An justificati possint legem divinam implere, quod adversarius absolute affirmat, nos de impletione imperfecta, inchoata damus, de perfecta negamus. Et postea explicans quid sit legem implere, Legem Dei implere, inquit, si absolute loquaris, est legi divinae obedientiam perfectam, sine ullo defectu, praestare, quod justificatos non posse nos docere fateor. Quibus subjungit nos docere homini justificato legem implere impossibile esse, non plane, ut nobis falso imponit Bellarminus, sed quoad legis ἀκρίβειαν, quae omnem defectum excludit, adeoque hominem in statu gratiae posse legem implere inchoate, hoc est, novam obedientiam legis, secundum omnia ejus praecepta inchoare: non posse vero implere absolute sine omni peccato.
english: Thesis XXX. So that no one can falsely allege that Protestants think otherwise, or that we are pinning on them a doctrine not their own, we will cite a few of their statements on the matter as a sample. To go through them all would be endless labour, and needless; besides, the matter is plain enough to anyone who pays attention.

Pareus, then, writing on Bellarmine's De justificatione, book 4, chapter 10, says: 'The question is whether the justified can fulfil the divine law. Our opponent affirms it absolutely; we grant it of an imperfect, begun fulfilment and deny it of a perfect one.' Later, explaining what fulfilling the law means, he says: 'To fulfil God's law, speaking absolutely, is to give the divine law a perfect obedience without any defect, and I confess we teach that the justified cannot do this.'

He goes on to say that we teach fulfilling the law is impossible for a justified person, not outright, as Bellarmine falsely charges us, but with respect to the law's exactness (ἀκρίβεια), which rules out every defect. A person in the state of grace can therefore fulfil the law in a begun way, that is, begin the new obedience of the law according to all its precepts, but cannot fulfil it absolutely, without any sin.

source_text: XXXI. Similia tradit Guilielmus Amesius in Bellarmino enervato tom. 4. lib. 6. c. 7. Nos, inquit, non docemus legem esse plane impossibilem homini, Adamo puta, ante lapsum, & postea Christo: necnon iis qui in Christo perfecte sanctificantur, sed de aliis, qui inchoatam tantum sanctificationem habent, ex ordinaria gratiae in ista vita dispensatione, ut legem divinam perfecte & exacte observent, nos dicimus hoc fieri non posse. Et postea, Respondens ad argumenta Bellarmini, concedit sanctos, qui in scriptura laudantur, observasse mandata proposito & conatu, non omnimodo effectu: quoad essentiam, non quoad complementum: quoad qualitatem sinceritatis, non quoad quantitatem intensionis, vel extensionis.
english: Thesis XXXI. William Ames says much the same in Bellarminus enervatus, volume 4, book 6, chapter 7: 'We do not teach that the law is simply impossible for man: for Adam, say, before the fall, and afterwards for Christ, or for those perfectly sanctified in Christ. But of others, whose sanctification is only begun under the ordinary dispensation of grace in this life, we say that they cannot keep the divine law perfectly and exactly.'

Later, replying to Bellarmine's arguments, he grants that the saints praised in Scripture kept the commandments in purpose and effort, though not completely in effect; in essence, not in completion; in the quality of sincerity, not in the quantity of intensity or extent.

source_text: XXXII. Eodem recidunt quae habet Joannes Davenantius de justitia actuali, c. 47. Etenim excutiens canonem illum Tridentinum, Si quis dixerit Dei praecepta homini justificato, & sub gratia constituto esse ad observandum impossibilia, anathema sit. Observatis velim, inquit, in hoc Canone fabricando artem Papisticam. Norunt adversarii nostros non negare Renatis diligentem observationem praeceptorum divinorum, sed negare perfectam illam & absolutam observationem, quae legi ita cumulate satisfacit, ut nullum ejus apicem violet; quae pactum legale ita adimplet, ut ejusdem beneficio vitae aeternae haereditatem consequatur. Frustra igitur haec anathematum fulmina contra Protestantes jaculantur, qui non asserunt esse impossibile Renatis observare praecepta Dei, studiose enim in illorum omnium observatione se exercent: sed esse impossibile observando justitiam legis adaequare, & omnem ἀνομίαν effugere.
english: Thesis XXXII. John Davenant's remarks on actual righteousness, chapter 47, come to the same thing. Examining the Tridentine canon 'If anyone says that God's precepts are impossible to keep for a man who is justified and placed under grace, let him be anathema,' he writes: 'Notice, please, the papist craft in framing this canon.

Our opponents know that our side does not deny the regenerate a diligent keeping of the divine precepts. What we deny is the perfect and absolute keeping that satisfies the law so fully that it breaks not one jot of it, and fulfils the legal covenant so completely that by virtue of it one gains the inheritance of eternal life.

So they hurl these thunderbolts of anathema at the Protestants in vain. Protestants do not claim that the regenerate cannot keep God's precepts, for they work hard at keeping all of them. They claim that it is impossible, by keeping them, to match the law's righteousness and escape all lawlessness (ἀνομία).'

source_text: XXXIII. Denique Robertus Baronius Scotus, in Academia Abredonensi Theologiae Professor, tractatum brevem edidit de possibilitate implendi legem Dei consideratam secundum ἐπιείκειαν Evangelicam, quem subjunxit, instar appendicis, disputationi de peccato mortali & veniali, ubi distinguit inter obedientiam quam lex Evangelio opposita exigit, ab eo qui, vi foederis legalis, ad vitam & foelicitatem pervenire contendit, juxta solennem illam clausulam fac & vives: Et inter legis obedientiam quam ipsum Evangelium, seu foedus gratiae, ut praecise necessariam ad salutem, a nobis postulat, & sine qua neminem ad vitam aeternam admittit. Quia, licet Evangelium maximis etiam ipsis peccatoribus, & legis transgressoribus, quos lex rigide sumpta damnat, & a vita excludit, spem salutis faciat, modo serio resipiscant, & Christum fide amplectantur, neminem tamen patitur vitam aeternam sperare, qui non acta poenitentia, verum aliquod & sincerum legi divinae obsequium praestet: quandoquidem declarat sine vitae sanctimonia neminem visurum esse Dominum. Posita vero ista distinctione duplicis obedientiae, unius quam foedus operum gratiae oppositum, alterius quam ipsum foedus gratiae postulat: affirmat Doctor ille obedientiam quam foedus operum, sive lex in rigore suo considerata, ab homine exigit, homini etiam Renato non esse possibilem, neque hoc respectu legem a fidelibus ullis impleri posse: sed eam legis obedientiam quam ipsum Evangelium necessarium esse ad salutem declarat, per ordinaria gratiae auxilia regenitis esse possibilem, illosque eatenus posse legem implere, & Dei Christique mandata servare. Etenim sectione prima modo dicti tractatus haec est ejus prima assertio, Ea legis obedientia quam foedus operum, seu lex secundum rigorem suum considerata, a nobis exigit ut praecise necessariam ad salutem, neque per naturae vires, neque per ordinaria gratiae auxilia, nobis est possibilis. Secunda vero assertio sic habet, Ea legis obedientia quam Evangelium, seu foedus gratiae a nobis ut praecise necessariam ad salutem exigit, per ordinaria gratiae auxilia nobis est possibilis. Imo omnia Dei mandata, sive legalia, sive Evangelica, sigillatim ex ea parte impleri possunt, ex qua a Deo nunc proponuntur, ut stricte & praecise obligativa, sub periculo & poena damnationis aeternae.
english: Thesis XXXIII. Finally Robert Baron, a Scot and professor of theology at the Academy of Aberdeen, published a short treatise on the possibility of fulfilling God's law considered according to evangelical equity (ἐπιείκεια), which he attached as an appendix to his disputation on mortal and venial sin. There he distinguishes two kinds of obedience.

The first is the obedience demanded by the law as opposed to the Gospel, from anyone who tries to reach life and happiness by virtue of the legal covenant, under its solemn clause 'Do and you will live'. The second is the obedience to the law that the Gospel itself, the covenant of grace, requires of us as strictly necessary for salvation, without which it admits no one to eternal life.

For although the Gospel offers hope of salvation even to the greatest sinners and lawbreakers, whom the law strictly taken condemns and shuts out of life, on condition that they truly repent and embrace Christ by faith, it allows no one to hope for eternal life who does not, after repenting, give the divine law some true and sincere obedience. It declares that without holiness of life no one will see the Lord.

With this distinction between the two obediences in place, one required by the covenant of works opposed to grace and the other by the covenant of grace itself, the doctor maintains the following. The obedience that the covenant of works, the law in its strictness, demands of man is not possible even for the regenerate, and in that respect no believer can fulfil the law. But the obedience to the law that the Gospel itself declares necessary for salvation is possible for the regenerate through the ordinary helps of grace, and to that extent they can fulfil the law and keep the commandments of God and of Christ.

Indeed, in the first section of that treatise his first assertion reads: 'The obedience to the law that the covenant of works, or the law considered in its strictness, demands of us as strictly necessary for salvation is possible for us neither by the powers of nature nor by the ordinary helps of grace.' His second assertion reads: 'The obedience to the law that the Gospel, or covenant of grace, demands of us as strictly necessary for salvation is possible for us through the ordinary helps of grace. Indeed all God's commandments, legal or evangelical, can be fulfilled one by one in the respect in which God now sets them before us as strictly and precisely binding, under threat and penalty of eternal damnation.'
